title: Du Bois-Reymond, Helmholtz, and the speed of the nerve impulse
text:
CHAPTER 2. ELECTRICITY AND THE NERVE
SECTION 2.2. DU BOIS-REYMOND, HELMHOLTZ, AND THE SPEED OF THE NERVE IMPULSE

From controversy to measurement

After Galvani and Volta, the question of animal electricity could only be settled with better instruments. The decisive tool was the galvanometer, a device that detects electric current by the deflection of a magnetized needle. Its principle depends on Hans Christian Oersted's discovery in 1820 that an electric current deflects a nearby compass needle. Within a few years, investigators built "multipliers" that wound many turns of wire around a needle to amplify the effect, and "astatic" designs that paired two needles with opposite orientations to cancel the effect of the Earth's magnetic field, greatly increasing sensitivity.

Carlo Matteucci

The Italian physicist Carlo Matteucci (1811 to 1868) used galvanometers to study bioelectricity in the 1830s and 1840s. He showed that a current flows between the cut surface and the intact surface of a muscle (the injury current Galvani's school had inferred). He also demonstrated the "rheoscopic frog": if the nerve of one frog nerve-muscle preparation is laid on a second muscle, and that second muscle is made to contract, the first preparation also twitches. This showed that a contracting muscle produces an electrical disturbance that can stimulate a nearby nerve. Matteucci's work is generally regarded as the first convincing demonstration with instruments that living muscle generates electrical currents.

Emil du Bois-Reymond and the "negative variation"

Emil du Bois-Reymond (1818 to 1896), working in Berlin as a student and later colleague of the physiologist Johannes Muller, took up the problem in the early 1840s. He built extremely sensitive galvanometers, some with thousands of turns of fine wire, and he developed non-polarizable electrodes to reduce the junction artifacts that had confused earlier work. His major work was Untersuchungen uber thierische Elektricitat ("Researches on animal electricity"), published in parts from 1848 onward.

His most important discovery was what he called the "negative variation" (negative Schwankung). He recorded the steady current flowing between the cut end and the intact surface of a nerve. When he stimulated the nerve, for example with a series of electrical shocks (tetanizing stimulation), the steady current decreased. The nerve's electrical state changed when it was active. This was the first recording, although indirect and blurred, of what we now call the action potential. Because the galvanometer needle was slow, it could not follow individual impulses; it showed only the average effect of many impulses, which appeared as a decrease in the resting current.

Du Bois-Reymond is often quoted, in loose paraphrase, as saying that he had realized the old dream of physicists and physiologists, the identity of the nerve principle with electricity. Translations of his exact words vary, so it is safer to say that he regarded his results as establishing that the nerve impulse is fundamentally an electrical phenomenon. He was also a strong advocate of a physical and chemical approach to physiology. Together with Hermann von Helmholtz, Ernst Brucke, and Carl Ludwig, he belonged to a group of German physiologists in the 1840s who were committed to explaining living processes in terms of physics and chemistry, rejecting appeals to a special "vital force."

Johannes Muller and the doctrine of specific nerve energies

Before we come to Helmholtz, we should mention a puzzle raised by their teacher, Johannes Muller (1801 to 1858). In his influential Handbook of Human Physiology (1830s), Muller set out the "law of specific nerve energies." The idea is that the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated, not on how it is stimulated. For example, pressing on the eye, or stimulating the optic nerve electrically, produces a sensation of light, not of pressure or electricity. Stimulating the auditory nerve produces sound. So the nerve fibers themselves, or the brain regions they connect to, determine what kind of experience results.

This principle is important for anyone thinking about information. It says that the brain interprets signals according to their source: a signal arriving on the optic nerve line is treated as visual. In modern terms, neural signals are labeled by their wiring, which is sometimes called a "labeled line" code. The signal on the wire (an electrical impulse) can be the same in every nerve; what differs is where it comes from and where it goes.

Muller also believed that the speed of the nerve impulse was probably too fast to be measured, perhaps comparable to the speed of light, and he expressed doubt that it would ever be measured in practice. Within a few years, his own student would measure it.

Hermann von Helmholtz measures the impulse

Hermann von Helmholtz (1821 to 1894) was one of the great scientists of the nineteenth century. He made fundamental contributions to physics (including a classic 1847 formulation of the conservation of energy), physiology, the theory of vision and hearing, and the philosophy of perception. He also invented the ophthalmoscope, a device for looking into the living eye.

In 1849 and 1850, while at Konigsberg, Helmholtz measured the speed at which the nerve impulse travels. His approach was ingenious and uses ideas that any instrumentation engineer would recognize.

He used a frog nerve-muscle preparation: the gastrocnemius (calf) muscle with its sciatic nerve. The idea was simple. Stimulate the nerve at a point near the muscle and measure the time until the muscle starts to contract. Then stimulate the nerve at a point farther from the muscle and measure the time again. The difference in times is the time the impulse takes to travel the extra length of nerve. Divide the extra length by the time difference and you have the conduction velocity.

The challenge was that the time differences are tiny, only a few thousandths of a second, which could not be measured with a clock. Helmholtz used two methods.

1. A ballistic galvanometer method, based on a technique introduced by Claude Pouillet. At the instant of stimulation, a circuit was closed, causing current to flow through a galvanometer. When the muscle began to contract, it broke the circuit. The total deflection of the galvanometer needle was proportional to the time the current flowed, so the deflection measured the time interval. This converts time into charge, which is integrated by the needle. An electronics engineer will recognize this as a time-to-amplitude conversion, the same principle used in some modern precision timing circuits.

2. A graphical method using a kymograph-like recorder: the contracting muscle moved a stylus that drew a trace on a rotating cylinder (in some versions, a smoked glass cylinder) moving at a known speed. Stimulating at two different points produced two curves shifted in time, and the horizontal shift between them gave the time difference.

Helmholtz found that the impulse in frog nerve travels at roughly 25 to 30 meters per second, depending on conditions and temperature. This is extraordinarily slow compared with electricity in a metal wire, which propagates at a substantial fraction of the speed of light. It is slower than a fast car on a highway. Helmholtz later carried out related reaction-time measurements on humans, with estimates for human nerve conduction velocity that were higher than in the frog, and he noted the variability of human measurements. (Modern values for the fastest human motor nerves are on the order of 50 to 70 meters per second, while thin unmyelinated fibers conduct at about 1 meter per second or less.)

Why the slow speed mattered

The result had several important consequences.

First, it showed that the nerve impulse is not simply electric current flowing through the nerve as through a copper wire. If it were, it would be essentially instantaneous over these distances. Something else, something slower and probably involving the material of the nerve itself, must be going on. This was a crucial clue that would only be fully understood in the twentieth century with the work of Hodgkin and Huxley.

Second, it brought the mind into the realm of measurable time. If nerve signals take measurable time to travel, then perception and action take measurable time. This opened the door to the measurement of mental processes. The Dutch physiologist Franciscus Donders, in the 1860s, developed the "subtractive method" for measuring the time taken by mental operations: by comparing reaction times on a simple task (press a button when you see a light) with those on a more complex task (press the button only for a red light), he estimated the time needed for the additional mental step. This is one of the foundations of experimental psychology and of the later field of cognitive psychology. Wilhelm Wundt, who founded one of the first psychology laboratories in Leipzig in 1879, had worked as Helmholtz's assistant in Heidelberg.

Third, it showed that the nervous system has latency, and therefore that any controller built on nerves must deal with delay. This is a central fact in motor control. If the signal from your hand to your brain and back takes tens of milliseconds, plus processing time, a purely feedback-driven controller would be too slow for fast movements. The brain must rely on prediction and feedforward control. We will meet this idea again in the context of internal models and predictive coding.

Bernstein and the membrane hypothesis

The next step came from Julius Bernstein (1839 to 1917), another student of du Bois-Reymond and later a professor at Halle. In 1868 Bernstein built a device called a "differential rheotome" (literally "current slicer"), which allowed him to sample the electrical state of a nerve at precisely controlled delays after a stimulus. The device used a rotating wheel with contacts: on each rotation, one contact delivered the stimulus, and another briefly connected the galvanometer to the nerve at a fixed delay. By repeating this many times at each delay and changing the delay step by step, he could reconstruct the time course of the negative variation, building up a picture of a brief electrical event lasting about a millisecond.

If you have used a sampling oscilloscope, you will recognize this exactly. A sampling oscilloscope reconstructs a fast repetitive waveform by taking one sample per repetition at a slowly shifting delay. Bernstein did the same thing mechanically in 1868. He is thus credited with the first recording of the time course of the action potential, and he measured its conduction velocity in a way that agreed with Helmholtz.

In 1902, Bernstein proposed the "membrane hypothesis." He suggested that nerve and muscle cells are surrounded by a membrane that is selectively permeable to potassium ions at rest. Because potassium is more concentrated inside the cell than outside, potassium ions tend to diffuse out, leaving the inside negatively charged. This creates the resting potential. He proposed that during excitation, the membrane temporarily loses its selectivity and becomes permeable to other ions, so that the potential collapses toward zero. This collapse was the negative variation.

Bernstein's hypothesis was partly right and partly wrong. He was right that the resting potential comes mainly from potassium and that excitation involves a change in membrane permeability. He was wrong in thinking that the potential merely collapses to zero. In 1939, Hodgkin and Huxley, and independently Kenneth Cole and Howard Curtis, recorded from inside squid giant axons and found that the membrane potential during the action potential overshoots zero, becoming positive inside. This overshoot could not be explained by a simple loss of selectivity. It required a selective increase in permeability to another ion, which turned out to be sodium. We will develop this in the next section and in chapter 5.

Bernstein's hypothesis also relied on the physical chemistry of ions in solution, especially the work of Walther Nernst, whose equation for the equilibrium potential of an ion was published in 1888 and 1889. This brings us directly to the physics of the membrane, the subject of section 2.3.

Bridge to AI: latency, sampling, and labeled lines

Three ideas in this section have direct parallels in AI and engineering.

Latency and prediction. Biological neurons are slow: conduction speeds of meters per second and synaptic delays of about a millisecond. Yet humans can catch a ball, play the piano, and recognize a face in a fraction of a second. Because the hardware is slow, the brain uses massive parallelism and prediction. Visual recognition of objects in primates can be fast enough that there is time for only a limited number of processing stages, which has been used as an argument that the first rapid wave of object recognition is largely feedforward. This argument helped motivate feedforward deep networks as models of the visual system. In robotics, controllers with delays face the same problem and solve it with predictive models, such as the Smith predictor or model predictive control. Modern reinforcement learning agents often learn predictive "world models" for related reasons.

Sampling. Bernstein's rheotome is a reminder that clever measurement design can overcome slow instruments. The same principle, sampling a repeatable signal at shifting delays, is used in equivalent-time sampling oscilloscopes. In neuroscience today, analog-to-digital converters sample neural signals at tens of kilohertz, and the raw data are processed by algorithms, often machine learning algorithms, to detect and classify spikes.

Labeled lines and embeddings. Muller's law of specific nerve energies says that meaning comes from which line carries a signal. In artificial neural networks, the meaning of a unit's activity also depends entirely on its connections: what it receives from and what it sends to. A unit in a network has no intrinsic meaning; its "meaning" is defined by its role in the network, which is learned. In modern networks, information is usually represented not in single labeled lines but in patterns across many units (distributed representations, or embeddings). The brain uses both: some pathways are fairly labeled (pain fibers, for example, though even that is debated), while higher brain areas use distributed population codes. We will explore this in the chapter on neural coding.

Summary

- Sensitive galvanometers made it possible to measure bioelectric currents directly. Matteucci showed currents in muscle; du Bois-Reymond discovered the "negative variation," the first indirect recording of the action potential.
- Johannes Muller proposed the law of specific nerve energies: the quality of a sensation depends on which nerve is stimulated.
- In 1849 and 1850 Helmholtz measured the conduction speed of frog nerve at about 25 to 30 meters per second, showing the impulse is far slower than electrical conduction in a wire.
- This made mental processes measurable in time and led to reaction-time studies by Donders and the rise of experimental psychology.
- Bernstein used a differential rheotome, essentially a mechanical sampling oscilloscope, to record the time course of the action potential (1868), and proposed the membrane hypothesis (1902).
- The overshoot of the action potential, discovered in 1939, showed Bernstein's theory was incomplete and pointed to sodium.
